title: What's the evidence-based alternative to prescribing sleep medication for older patients? I'm trying to find something with real clinical backing, not just a meditation app.
summary: CBT-I is the clinically proven, guideline-recommended alternative to sleep medication for older patients, and it outperforms pills in long-term studies. Here's what the research says and where to find programs with real clinical backing.
body_text: Bottom Line Up Front The evidence-based alternative to pharmacotherapy for chronic insomnia in older patients is multicomponent Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I). The American College of Physicians gives it a strong recommendation as first-line treatment before any medication. The AASM clinical practice guideline reserves its only "strong" recommendation for multicomponent CBT-I. Effect sizes in 2024–2025 meta-analyses reach Hedges' g = 0.98–1.87 in real-world settings — comparable to or exceeding pharmacological effect sizes, with no adverse events and durable remission. Sleep Reset delivers CBT-I through dedicated human coaches with board-certified sleep physician oversight, available without waitlists. The Guideline Position: What Multiple Societies Now Agree On This is no longer a contested area of clinical practice. The following organizations have issued explicit recommendations placing CBT-I above pharmacotherapy as initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in adults, including older adults: Organization Recommendation Strength Source American College of Physicians All adult patients should receive CBT-I as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. Pharmacotherapy should be added only via shared decision-making in patients where CBT-I alone was unsuccessful. Strong — moderate-quality evidence Annals of Internal Medicine, 2016 American Academy of Sleep Medicine Multicomponent CBT-I is the only treatment receiving a "strong" recommendation. All individual pharmacological agents receive only "weak" recommendations. Medication should be considered mainly in patients unable to participate in CBT-I or who remain symptomatic after it. Strong for CBT-I; weak for all medications AASM CPG, 2021 American Geriatrics Society (Beers Criteria) Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) should be avoided for insomnia in older adults. All increase risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents. CBT-I is the indicated first-line approach. Avoid — explicit Beers listing for all Z-drugs and BZDs in elderly AGS Beers Criteria, 2023 update World Sleep Society Endorsed AASM strong recommendation for multicomponent CBT-I as the treatment of choice for insomnia disorder. Strong recommendation applies to patients with or without comorbid psychiatric and medical conditions. Strong — international endorsement Sleep Medicine, 2023 European Insomnia Guideline CBT-I recommended as first-line treatment. Pharmacotherapy only as adjunct or second-line. Guideline updated 2023 to reflect growing digital CBT-I evidence. First-line recommendation European Insomnia Guideline, 2023 The clinical consensus is unambiguous. CBT-I is the treatment of choice for chronic insomnia in older adults. The question is not whether to recommend it, but how to make it accessible to patients who need it. The Evidence Base: Current Effect Sizes CBT-I is among the most thoroughly investigated non-pharmacological treatments in sleep medicine. The evidence base now spans hundreds of randomized controlled trials and multiple large-scale meta-analyses, several published in 2024 and 2025. Multicomponent CBT-I: headline findings A 2024 component network meta-analysis in JAMA Psychiatry synthesized 241 trials and 31,452 participants. Multicomponent CBT-I had the highest likelihood of remission at OR 2.50 (95% CI 1.93–3.24) compared to psychoeducation, outperforming all individual components and all passive controls. A December 2025 meta-analysis in Cognitive Behaviour Therapy — covering 32 real-world effectiveness studies and 5,231 participants — reported very large within-group effect sizes for insomnia severity at post-treatment (Hedges' g = 1.87) and follow-up (Hedges' g = 1.68, mean 12 months post-treatment), with remission rates of 45% at post-treatment and 51% at follow-up. These are real-world clinical care settings, not efficacy-optimized RCT conditions. A November 2025 meta-analysis in JAMA Internal Medicine specifically examined CBT-I in 67 RCTs of patients with chronic disease comorbidities (cancer, chronic pain, cardiovascular disease, IBS, stroke) — a population directly relevant to older adults. CBT-I was associated with insomnia severity improvement of g = 0.98 (95% CI, 0.81–1.16), sleep efficiency g = 0.77, and sleep onset latency g = 0.64, with a mean dropout rate of 13.3% — comparable to pharmacological trials. Effect sizes were consistent across disease subgroups. Specifically in older adult populations A July 2025 RCT in npj Digital Medicine , conducted at the University of Virginia, enrolled 311 participants aged 55–95 in a tailored digital CBT-I program. Both the self-guided and coach-supported arms showed significant improvements in insomnia severity, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, and fatigue compared to controls at post-treatment, 6-month, and 12-month follow-up. This is among the most age-inclusive CBT-I trials conducted to date. A 2025 secondary analysis in Aging & Mental Health pooled three digital CBT-I RCTs in adults aged 65 and older (N = 315). Digital CBT-I significantly improved insomnia, anxiety, and depression scores at post-treatment and at 24-week follow-up. These secondary mental health benefits are particularly relevant given the high comorbidity burden in this population. A 2024 study in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society evaluated CBT-I in community-dwelling older veterans (mean age 72.1 years) with chronic insomnia and found improvement in insomnia severity, sleep quality, fatigue, and daytime sleepiness — with patients experiencing higher chronic pain showing greater insomnia improvement, not less. Which CBT-I Components Drive Outcomes? For prescribers evaluating program quality, the component-level evidence matters. A 2024 network meta-analysis in Clinical Psychology Review (80 studies, 15,351 participants) found that sleep restriction therapy was the most effective single component for insomnia severity (d = −0.45; 95% CI −0.63 to −0.36), improving subjective sleep continuity, sleep onset latency, WASO, and sleep efficiency. Stimulus control therapy was the most effective for improving total sleep time. Relaxation therapy, psychoeducation, and sleep hygiene alone showed no significant effects on insomnia severity as stand-alone components. The clinical implication: a program that relies primarily on sleep hygiene education or relaxation techniques — regardless of how it is branded — is not delivering the treatment components with demonstrated efficacy. Effective CBT-I must include sleep restriction and stimulus control, both of which require patient adherence to protocols that are difficult to maintain without structured guidance. CBT-I vs Pharmacotherapy: Comparative Effectiveness Dimension CBT-I Pharmacotherapy (Z-drugs, BZDs) Pharmacotherapy (DORAs) Onset of benefit 2–3 weeks for initial improvement; full benefit 6–8 weeks Days Days Long-term durability Sustained and often improving at 12-month follow-up; one RCT showed sustained benefit at 10-year follow-up Tolerance develops; insomnia returns on discontinuation; rebound worsening Sustained while on medication; discontinuation outcomes not well established long-term Fall / dizziness risk in older adults None — no adverse event signal in RCTs High: 3–4× increased fall risk; 1.92× relative risk of hip fracture; on AGS Beers list Lower than Z-drugs; narcolepsy-like symptoms reported; somnolence dose-dependent Cognitive effects Improves cognitive performance via improved sleep quality 5× increased memory loss, confusion, and disorientation in older adults; associated with Alzheimer's risk at high cumulative doses Better cognitive profile than Z-drugs; less residual next-day impairment Dependency risk None High — 68% of zolpidem users take it long-term despite short-term-only approval; median 192 days of supply in one cohort study Low (Schedule IV); misuse potential present Comorbidity benefit Secondary improvements in depression (SMD −0.42) and anxiety (SMD −0.29); effective across chronic disease populations May exacerbate depression; linked to increased suicidal ideation at OR 2.08 in one meta-analysis Emerging data on anxiety benefits; early research on dementia populations Supports deprescribing Yes — concurrent CBT-I significantly increases successful hypnotic discontinuation rates; AASM guidelines specifically note CBT-I facilitates medication tapering N/A N/A The Access Problem — and How Digital CBT-I Addresses It The primary barrier to CBT-I in clinical practice is not evidence — it is access. Behavioral sleep medicine specialists are scarce; waitlists commonly run 3–6 months. Primary care physicians frequently lack the training time to deliver CBT-I themselves, and referring patients to sleep psychologists in many regions is simply not practical. The AASM explicitly recommends digital CBT-I as a valuable resource when in-person care is unavailable or waitlists are prohibitive — followed by therapist-delivered CBT-I when access becomes available. A March 2025 meta-analysis in npj Digital Medicine covering 29 RCTs and 9,475 participants found fully automated digital CBT-I produces moderate to large effect sizes on insomnia severity — though it is less effective than therapist-assisted CBT-I, reinforcing the value of human guidance in the protocol. The clinical distinction between digital CBT-I programs matters. Automated platforms deliver structured content but cannot adapt to individual patient presentations in real time. Coached platforms — where a human reviews the patient's sleep diary and adjusts the protocol week by week — more closely replicate the adaptive individualization of in-person treatment. This is particularly relevant for older adults, who often present with comorbidities, polypharmacy, and a concurrent medication taper that requires more nuanced management than a fixed algorithm can provide. Where Sleep Reset Fits in a Clinical Workflow Sleep Reset is an appropriate referral for older patients presenting with chronic insomnia who need a structured, evidence-based behavioral treatment and where in-person CBT-I is unavailable, impractical, or delayed by waitlists. It is also well-suited for patients currently on sleep medication for whom deprescribing is a clinical goal. Several features distinguish it from general digital wellness apps or basic automated CBT-I platforms: Feature Sleep Reset Typical automated digital CBT-I (Sleepio, etc.) Meditation / wellness apps CBT-I protocol (sleep restriction + stimulus control) ✓ Yes — full multicomponent ✓ Yes ✗ No — relaxation only Dedicated human sleep coach ✓ Yes — assigned, reviews daily sleep diary ✗ No — algorithm-driven ✗ No Board-certified sleep physician oversight ✓ Yes — licensed sleep medicine clinicians ✗ No ✗ No Home sleep testing for apnea ✓ Yes — physician-interpreted ✗ No ✗ No Supports concurrent medication taper ✓ Yes — designed for concurrent use with prescribing physician Partially — no clinical oversight ✗ No Access Immediate — no waitlist Immediate — no waitlist Immediate Cost / coverage CBT-I program: out-of-pocket, HSA/FSA eligible. Clinical services (clinician visits, home sleep testing, apnea care): covered by select insurers including Aetna, BCBS, Anthem. Check eligibility. Employer plans; SleepioRx via CMS DMHT codes (Jan 2025) Subscription; not covered Clinical Considerations Specific to Older Patients Sleep restriction in elderly patients — adjusting the protocol Sleep restriction is the most effective and most demanding CBT-I component. In older adults, the standard protocol requires modification: the minimum prescribed sleep window should not fall below 5.5 hours (versus the 5-hour floor used in younger adults), and titration should proceed more gradually — typically in 15-minute increments every 5–7 days rather than weekly. A human coach who understands the patient's baseline, comorbidities, and medication status is essential for calibrating this safely. The Sleep Reset approach to sleep restriction accounts for these age-related adjustments. Screening for comorbid sleep apnea before or alongside CBT-I Sleep apnea is significantly underdiagnosed in older adults and frequently presents as insomnia — particularly sleep maintenance insomnia with daytime fatigue. Initiating CBT-I without ruling out obstructive sleep apnea in patients who present with relevant risk factors (male sex, obesity, witnessed apneas, hypertension, large neck circumference, or refractory insomnia) risks treating the wrong condition. Sleep Reset's integrated home sleep testing allows this to be evaluated concurrently rather than as a prerequisite that delays behavioral treatment. Managing the medication taper concurrently with CBT-I The AASM clinical guidelines on insomnia management explicitly state that "medication tapering and discontinuation are facilitated by CBT-I" and recommend that "whenever possible, patients should receive an adequate trial of cognitive behavioral treatment during long-term pharmacotherapy." Starting CBT-I before or at the time of initiating a taper is superior to stopping medication first and hoping sleep improves. The prescribing physician manages the taper rate; Sleep Reset's coach manages the behavioral protocol — the two run in parallel under a shared patient understanding. Patients with cognitive impairment Standard CBT-I requires sufficient cognitive capacity to engage with sleep diaries, follow behavioral instructions, and process psychoeducation. Patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) can often complete modified CBT-I with appropriate support, but those with moderate or severe dementia require alternative approaches. A January 2026 pilot study in Brain Sciences developed and evaluated a clinician-supported mobile CBT-I app specifically designed for older adults with MCI, demonstrating feasibility and early efficacy signals. Patients with more significant cognitive decline should be evaluated individually; CBT-I is not contraindicated in MCI but may require clinical adaptation. Referring Patients to Sleep Reset: What to Tell Them For many older patients, "therapy" for sleep raises immediate questions. The framing that tends to work clinically: CBT-I is not psychotherapy for an emotional problem — it is a structured behavioral protocol for a physiological one. The techniques (particularly sleep restriction) can feel harder in the first 1–2 weeks before improving. Setting this expectation upfront significantly reduces dropout. It can be used alongside their current medication; they do not need to stop anything before starting. A real human coach reviews their progress daily and adjusts the protocol — this is not a meditation app or a tip sheet. The CBT-I program is out-of-pocket and HSA/FSA eligible. Insurance covers the clinical services component — clinician visits and sleep apnea-related care. Patients can take a free sleep assessment at Sleep Reset to identify their specific insomnia profile and be matched with an appropriate coach before committing to the program. Frequently Asked Questions From Clinicians Does CBT-I work in patients with significant medical comorbidities? Yes. The November 2025 JAMA Internal Medicine meta-analysis of 67 RCTs in chronic disease populations found CBT-I effect sizes for insomnia severity of g = 0.98 — comparable to results in otherwise healthy adults. Cancer, chronic pain, cardiovascular disease, IBS, and stroke were all represented. Efficacy was consistent across disease subgroups. Dropout rates were low (mean 13.3%). The recommendation against CBT-I in patients with comorbidities is not supported by the current evidence base. What about patients with comorbid depression or anxiety? CBT-I improves insomnia and has secondary benefits on depression and anxiety — a meta-analysis of digital CBT-I in patients with both insomnia and mood symptoms found SMD = −0.42 for depressive symptoms and SMD = −0.29 for anxiety symptoms at post-treatment, alongside a large effect on insomnia (SMD = −0.76). Treating insomnia directly may alleviate pressure on concurrent pharmacological management of mood disorders. In patients where the psychiatric presentation is primary and severe, concurrent specialist involvement is appropriate. Is there a risk of adverse effects from sleep restriction in older adults? Sleep restriction can temporarily increase daytime sleepiness in the first 1–2 weeks. This is expected and is the mechanism of the treatment. In older adults, a minimum sleep window of 5.5 hours is recommended rather than 5 hours, and titration should be more gradual. There is no evidence of serious adverse events from CBT-I in elderly populations across the RCT literature — a significant contrast to the adverse event profile of pharmacotherapy in this group. What is the evidence for CBT-I facilitating hypnotic discontinuation specifically? Multiple studies have demonstrated that concurrent CBT-I significantly increases successful hypnotic discontinuation rates compared to taper alone. The AASM and European Insomnia Guidelines both explicitly state that CBT-I facilitates medication tapering. A 2025 Lancet microsimulation study modeled the outcomes of eliminating prescription sleep medication in 15.3 million US adults over 50 — finding an 8.5% reduction in lifetime falls, 2.1% reduction in cognitive impairment, 0.11 additional life years, and $6,600 per-person net savings ($101 billion aggregate). CBT-I is the clinical mechanism by which that transition is made sustainable.

title: From Reactive to Real-Time: Rethinking Finance Visibility in Modern Organizations

We’ll also show how Boya’s live dashboard equips organizations with the tools to monitor, control, and forecast spend in real time. ‍ The Visibility Gap in Traditional Finance Processes ‍ ‍ According to a 2023 survey by Gartner, 60% of finance leaders cite delayed visibility into expenses as a top challenge impacting cash flow management . This challenge is amplified in organizations with decentralized teams, multiple payment channels (cards, mobile wallets, bank transfers), and fast-paced procurement needs. Traditionally, businesses rely on static reports: Spreadsheets updated days or weeks later Delayed expense claims and reconciliations Manual budget monitoring that fails to capture ongoing shifts The result? Leadership often learns about overspending after it’s too late to course-correct. Budget owners can’t confidently track spend against targets, and finance teams spend more time investigating issues than driving strategy. ‍ Why Real-Time Spend Visibility Matters ‍ ‍ The shift to real-time spend visibility delivers three key benefits: ✅ Better Forecasting : When you can see every transaction as it happens, cash flow forecasting becomes more accurate. You can adjust spending plans immediately based on real-time trends rather than outdated reports. ✅ Tighter Cost Control : With live transaction data, managers can spot overspending early, freeze budgets if needed, or adjust allocations on the fly. It also minimizes the risk of fraudulent or non-compliant spending going unnoticed. ✅ Improved Accountability : Department heads, team leads, and even individual employees get visibility into their spending patterns, making budget ownership a daily practice—not a month-end surprise. Whether it’s noticing rising travel costs mid-month or proactively tightening vendor payments, Boya shifts finance teams from firefighting to forecasting . ‍ The Strategic Payoff: Scale with Confidence ‍ ‍ In a previous blog, Scaling Your Business with Effective Expense Management , we explored how scaling businesses often outgrow traditional finance processes. Without timely visibility, the risks of uncontrolled spending, cash flow issues, and poor unit economics multiply rapidly. Real-time visibility is the antidote: Founders get peace of mind knowing cash runway is accurate CFOs can confidently report numbers to investors Managers can optimize spending decisions without waiting for finance It’s not just about seeing spend—it’s about steering the company’s financial health in real time. ‍ Conclusion: Moving from Reactive to Proactive Finance In 2025, operating with a 30-day financial delay is no longer acceptable. Real-time spend visibility isn’t a nice-to-have—it’s a competitive advantage. Companies that embrace live expense monitoring unlock sharper forecasts, tighter controls, and greater accountability across teams. Boya’s dashboard empowers organizations to move from reactive to proactive, giving every stakeholder—from finance teams to department heads—the tools to drive smarter, faster decisions. 💡 Ready to see how real-time spend visibility can transform your business? title: A Technical Breakdown of Jolt's Cryptography (and the exploit)
summary: The mathematics of the missing Dory commitments behind the Jolt exploit.
body_text: Breaking Down Jolt Cryptography The Mathematics Behind the Exploit Jul 13, 2026 #zkvm #cryptography This is a technical analysis of the Dory vulnerability that was found and poc’d by our agent. This blog goes much deeper into the mathematics behind how the exploit actually worked. If you’ve landed in the wrong blog, you can read how our AI found it here . TL;DR Ordering of Fiat-Shamir in Sumcheck Missing constraint in the Dory proving library Exploiting the constraint and backsolving from the Fiat-Shamir ordering is_seven(6) == true (6 == 7) About Us At Veria Labs, we build AI pentesting agents that automatically find and fix security vulnerabilities in your application. Founded by members of the #1 competitive hacking team in the U.S., we’ve found critical vulnerabilities in every company we’ve worked with, from small startups to enterprise giants. Think we can help secure your systems? We’d love to chat! Book a call here . What is Jolt? We’ve covered Jolt in our other blog but in brief, Jolt is a zkVM for RISC-V built as a general purpose zkVM for proving arbitrary executions. While it can be used as a standalone library, Jolt is expected to be the backbone of the new Zero L1 chain currently being developed by LayerZero. Jolt will facilitate private payments on the Zero network. This allows anyone to verify transactions without seeing details like wallet addresses, amounts, etc. Vulnerability Details This section covers the math, the vulnerabilities, and how they were chained. As always, this may get quite messy. Background From a program to polynomials : A zkVM proves “this program ran correctly and produced this output.” Jolt encodes the execution trace as a family of multilinear polynomials {Pi}i∈[m] over the BN254 scalar field 𝔽=𝔽r, where each Pi:𝔽n→𝔽 is the multilinear extension of its values on the boolean hypercube, Pi(𝐱)=∑𝐛∈{0,1}nPi(𝐛)∏k=1n(xkbk+(1−xk)(1−bk)),𝐱∈𝔽n. Checking the program reduces to checking a system of claims over the {Pi}. Sumcheck. The sumcheck step certifies that a polynomial g=∑iλigi sums to a claimed value C over the hypercube without the verifier recomputing the sum: C=?∑𝐱∈{0,1}ng(𝐱),λi=ℋ(τ)∈𝔽. It runs one variable at a time. In round j the prover sends the univariate restriction gj(X)=∑𝐱∈{0,1}n−jg(r1,…,rj−1,X,𝐱), the verifier enforces the fold gj(0)+gj(1)=cj−1 against the running claim, samples a challenge rj∈𝔽, and updates cj=gj(rj). After n rounds the protocol collapses to a vector of opening claims at the random point 𝐫=(r1,…,rn). {Pi(𝐫)=vi}i∈[m],vi∈𝔽, Sumcheck is interactive however. To turn this non-interactive, Jolt applies a Fiat-Shamir transcript across all steps to sample the randomness. Jolt derives every challenge by hashing the running transcript τ of prover messages: rj=ℋ(τ<j). Security relies on this binding invariant. Anything that can change whether the proof is accepted must be absorbed into τ before the challenge that depends on it: ∀accept-relevant w:w→τ before r=ℋ(τ). Polynomial commitments ( Dory ). The openings Pi(𝐫)=vi are discharged by a polynomial commitment scheme. Jolt batches its polynomials under powers of a challenge γ into one instance (𝒞∗,𝐫,y∗) with 𝒞∗=∑iγi𝒞i, and proves it with Dory. Dory is a pairing based scheme, also developed by a16z, over 𝔾1,𝔾2,𝔾T with a pairing e:𝔾1×𝔾2→𝔾T. Dory asserts that a committed polynomial 𝒞∈𝔾T satisfies P(𝐳)=y with a final pairing identity of the form ∏ke(Lk(𝐳),Rk)=𝒞⋅e(⋅,e2), where e2∈𝔾2 encodes the claimed value. The Ordering of Fiat-Shamir in Sumcheck The ZK sumcheck fixes its random challenges before the prover commits to the hidden output claims. The batching coefficients λ are drawn up front, the round polynomials are folded to produce 𝐫, and only afterwards are the hidden output claims added into the transcript: 1 let batching_coeffs = transcript . challenge_vector (sumcheck_instances . len ()); // λ ← H(τ) [early] 2 // … n sumcheck rounds fold r_1..r_n out of τ … 3 let oc_committed = pedersen_gens . commit_chunked ( & output_claim_values, rng); // Com(v_i; ρ_i) 4 transcript . append_commitments ( b"output_claims_coms" , & output_claims_commitments); // τ += Com(v) [late] By the time the openings 𝖢𝗈𝗆(vi;ρi) enter τ, every challenge that will test them is fixed. Write 𝝌=(λ,𝐫,…) for those challenges and Φ(𝐯,𝝌)=0 for the BlindFold output constraint the openings must satisfy. There’s no way around this ordering: the output claims are values p(𝐫), and 𝐫 (like λ) is the sumcheck’s challenge stream, so the claims don’t exist until the challenges that produce them are already drawn. Binding the openings is intended to be left entirely to the Stage 8 opening proof. Technically, that does give a modified prover some help. With 𝝌 known first, and Φ affine in each opening, changing one coordinate vk by δ moves the constraint along a straight line, Φ(𝐯+δ,𝐞k,,𝝌);=;Φ(𝐯,𝝌)+δ⋅∂vkΦ,∂vkΦ≠0, so the offset that lands it back on zero is just δ⋆=−,Φ(𝐯,𝝌)/∂vkΦ. The prover shifts the hidden opening and re-commits; the only thing that changes is the freshly-formed 𝖢𝗈𝗆(vk;ρk), which nothing has constrained yet: 1 let delta_i = (target_output_claim - base_eval) * derivative_i . inverse () . unwrap (); // δ* = -Φ/∂Φ 2 output_claim_values[output_index] += delta_i; // v_k ↦ v_k + δ* 3 * opening_value += delta_i; But by design this isn’t supposed to work: the Stage 8 Dory opening is supposed to reject any 𝐯 whose openings don’t match the real polynomials Pi at 𝐫. The Vulnerability: Missing Constraint in Dory Dependency Jolt calls the Dory library for all proving/verifying related to Dory. In Dory’s zk verifier, it never ties the proof to the point it is supposed to be evaluated at. Stage 8 first collapses all the committed polynomials into a joint opening (𝒞∗, 𝐫, y∗) with 𝒞∗=∑iγi𝒞i, and hands it to verify_zk with the point 𝐫 but no value, since in ZK the evaluation stays concealed as ycom=𝖢𝗈𝗆(y∗;⋅): 1 let hiding_evaluation_commitment = PCS :: verify_zk ( 2 & joint_commitment, pcs_opening_point . as_slice (), // (C*, r) ; no y* 3 & proof . joint_opening_proof, & preprocessing . pcs_setup, transcript) ? ; Following this call into the Dory function dory-pcs::verify_evaluation_proof in the dependency, the whole thing turns on a single group element e2∈𝔾2 that anchors the final pairing identity. In the transparent (non-ZK) path, e2 is built from the claimed value which ties both the value y and the point 𝐳 into the equation: (𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭)e2=y⋅g2,verify ∏ke(Lk(𝐳),Rk)=𝒞⋅e(⋅,e2). In ZK mode though, it reads e2 from the proof and discards y entirely: (𝐳𝐤)e2←π.e2 (prover-chosen),y unused,ycom←π.ycom. 1 #[cfg(feature = "zk" )] 2 let (e2, is_zk) = match ( & proof . e2, & proof . y_com) { 3 ( Some (pe2), Some (yc)) => { /* sub-proofs about y_com only */ ( * pe2, true ) } 4 ( None , None ) => (setup . g2_0 . scale ( & evaluation), false ), 5 _ => return Err ( DoryError :: InvalidProof ), 6 }; 7 #[cfg(not(feature = "zk" ))] 8 let (e2, _is_zk) = (setup . g2_0 . scale ( & evaluation), false ); // e2 binds `evaluation` The side proofs check that ycom is a well formed commitment, but they never check that it actually commits to P∗(𝐳). So with e2 as a free group element the prover supplies, the acceptance relation stops depending on 𝐳 altogether: ∃π:V(𝒞∗,𝐳,π)=1 for every 𝐳∈𝔽n. The Full Exploit For the PoC, our agent setup a simple Rust program of: 1 fn is_seven (x : u64 ) -> bool { 2 x == 7 3 } with the goal of forging a proof to claim is_seven(6) == true . Since the vulnerability allows an attacker to forge a Dory proof, the first observation on the ordering of the sumcheck can be backsolved before abusing the Dory commitment. The attack runs in 2 main steps. Let 𝐲∗∈{0,1}8 be the public output region. In an honest case: 𝗂𝗌_𝗌𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗇(6) produces y0∗=0 (false). First, flip the public output bit (from false to true) and rewrite the single store instruction that writes it, so the trace claims the flipped value: y0∗↦y0∗⊕︎1,rewrite the unique 𝖲𝖡/𝖲𝖧/𝖲𝖶/𝖲𝖣→𝚙𝚘𝚜𝚝_𝚟𝚊𝚕𝚞𝚎. The witness is now internally inconsistent since the BlindFold constraint breaks (Φ(𝐯,𝝌)≠0) An honest prover would abort on 𝐀𝐳∘𝐁𝐳≠𝐂𝐳. Because the sumcheck never bound the claim values, solve for the offset that puts the broken constraint back to zero and shift the hidden output opening by it: δ∗=−Φ(𝐯,𝝌)/∂vkΦ,vk↦vk+δ∗ ⇒ Φ=0,Ξ(⋅) fixed. The prover now holds a coherent but false claim set, with a forged joint value y^∗≠P∗(𝐫). The forged claim no longer matches the real polynomial at the honest point. But a multilinear polynomial is degree ≤1 in each coordinate, so its value moves linearly as you sweep one coordinate. This means you can solve for a single alternate coordinate rℓ′ at which the real polynomial hits the forged value exactly: 𝐫′=𝐫 with rℓ′=y^∗−P∗(𝐫|zℓ=0)P∗(𝐫|zℓ=1)−P∗(𝐫|zℓ=0) ⟹ P∗(𝐫′)=y^∗. The prover emits a perfectly honest Dory opening at this wrong point, π←𝗈𝗉𝖾𝗇_𝗓𝗄(P∗,𝐫′). The verifier checks at the honest point 𝐫. Since Dory’s ZK check ignores the point, it accepts anyway (V(𝒞∗,𝐫,π)=1). This was run against an unchanged verifier and both honest and forged proofs: 𝚑𝚘𝚗𝚎𝚜𝚝.𝚋𝚒𝚗→𝖮𝗄 (y0∗=0),𝚙𝚘𝚌.𝚋𝚒𝚗→𝖮𝗄 (y0∗=1):6=7. Impact in the zkVM This is a total break of soundness in ZK mode. For an arbitrary false statement S there exists an constructible π with 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒zk(S,π)=1, against the unchanged verifier. The transparent path, binding both y (via e2=y⋅g2) and 𝐳, is unaffected. Since Jolt is used as a general purpose zkVM as well as being the backbone of the Zero L1 chain, this makes it the highest impact for a zkVM. On the blockchain, depending on how it will be used, can most likely be used to forge false transactions or introduce an infinite mint. Remediation Patching the Dory vulnerability can be done in either the library or Jolt itself. Bind the opening point. The cleanest fix would be to directly patch this on the Dory library side. That said, there is a comment that claims the caller must bind this before calling any Dory functions. So, to fix this on the Jolt side, we can apply the patch: 1 --- a/crates/jolt-dory/src/scheme.rs 2 +++ b/crates/jolt-dory/src/scheme.rs 3 @@ fn open_zk(poly, point, _eval, setup, hint, transcript) { 4 let ark_point: Vec<ArkFr> = point.iter().rev().map(jolt_fr_to_ark).collect(); 5 + // Bind the opening point before Dory derives its challenges. 6 + transcript.append(&LabelWithCount(b"zk_dory_point_bind", point.len() as u64)); 7 + for p in point { 8 + p.append_to_transcript(transcript); 9 + } 10 let mut dory_transcript = JoltToDoryTranscript::new(transcript); 1 --- a/crates/jolt-dory/src/scheme.rs 2 +++ b/crates/jolt-dory/src/scheme.rs 3 @@ fn verify_zk(commitment, point, proof, setup, transcript) { 4 let ark_commitment = jolt_gt_to_ark(&commitment.0); 5 + // Mirror the prover: bind the same point before verification draws challenges. 6 + transcript.append(&LabelWithCount(b"zk_dory_point_bind", point.len() as u64)); 7 + for p in point { 8 + p.append_to_transcript(transcript); 9 + } 10 let mut dory_transcript = JoltToDoryTranscript::new(transcript); With this in place an honest proof still verifies, and a proof produced at a different point is rejected: verify at correct point = Ok(...) verify at wrong point = Err(VerificationFailed) Conclusion This is a result of feature and a missing check that were chained together to fulfill the full exploit chain. While each on there own are not exploitable, exploiting both at the same time allows for complete proof forgery. The Dory vulnerability was reported to a16z which was quickly patched. Fixes from the team are listed here: On the Jolt side, https://github.com/a16z/jolt/pull/1664 and on the Dory side: https://github.com/a16z/dory/pull/23 PoC All files related to the PoC can be found in this GitHub repo: https://github.com/verialabs/Jolt-PoC

title: The Science of Workout Variety: Why It Keeps You Consistent
summary: Does workout variety help you stay consistent? Science says yes. Here are 5 research-backed reasons variety beats boredom and makes the habit stick.
body_text: The Science of Workout Variety: 5 Reasons Doing Something Different Helps You Stay Consistent Variety is not a luxury. It is the mechanism that keeps a workout habit alive. Short answer: Yes, workout variety helps you stay consistent. Research links varied training to better exercise adherence, mostly because it fights the boredom that makes people quit. Mixing up how you train (different machines, formats, and intensities) keeps you mentally engaged and physically progressing, so the habit actually sticks. Here is the part nobody tells you: if you have quit a workout routine before, it was probably not a willpower problem. Most fitness equipment is engineered to be boring, while the phone in your pocket is engineered to be irresistible. You were never in a fair fight. The good news is that the same science that explains why you quit also points to a fix, and it is not "try harder." It is variety. In this article Does workout variety really help you stay consistent? Why most people quit (and why it is not willpower) 5 science-backed reasons variety keeps you consistent But isn't consistency more important than variety? How to get variety without buying five machines Frequently asked questions Does workout variety really help you stay consistent? It does, and the effect is bigger than most people expect. Boredom is one of the most reliable predictors of dropping out of a fitness program, and variety is the direct antidote. When researchers compare high-variety and low-variety programs, the high-variety groups tend to stick with it longer, and the effect is driven by how much variety people feel they are getting, not just what is on paper. The chain is simple: people repeat what they enjoy, variety increases enjoyment, enjoyment increases adherence, and adherence is what creates results. A recent 2024 study found that adding structured variety to a routine improved motivation, self-efficacy, and how positively people felt about exercise, and they reported feeling more autonomous and confident too. Novelty is also doing something in your brain. New challenges nudge the dopamine system that drives learning and reward , which is a big reason a fresh workout feels more engaging than the fiftieth identical session. Why most people quit (and why it is not willpower) Roughly half of new gym members quit within six months, and a large share of memberships go essentially unused. Home equipment tells the same story. The rower, the bike, or the treadmill arrives with big plans attached, and by month two it has quietly become an expensive clothes rack. That moment has a name: the motivation cliff. The cliff is not a character flaw. It is what happens when repetitive equipment collides with a brain that craves novelty. Do the same 20 minutes of steady cardio every day and your body adapts, the challenge fades, and your mind checks out. This is where variety stops being a "nice to have" and becomes the thing that keeps you showing up. It is also why Aviron built game psychology into the machine itself, and why 92% of Aviron members are still working out a year later , a number that looks almost impossible next to those industry dropout rates. A rower brings a completely different stimulus than a run or a ride: full-body, low-impact, and easy to make playful. The variety engine, in one machine Aviron Strong Rower Full-body, low-impact rowing with 1,000+ games, classes, and scenic routes so no two sessions feel the same. Free 30-day home trial · Financing available Shop the Strong Rower → 5 science-backed reasons variety keeps you consistent 1. It kills boredom, the number one reason people quit Boredom is not a minor annoyance. It is a leading driver of dropout. Variety keeps the experience novel, and novelty keeps your brain's reward system switched on. That is the difference between "I have to work out" and "I get to play the next level." 2. It breaks plateaus so you keep seeing results Your body follows the SAID principle: Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands. Do the same thing and you adapt to exactly that thing, then progress stalls. Changing the movement, tempo, or intensity is a form of progressive overload. In fact, groups that varied their training have made greater gains in muscle size and strength than those who repeated an identical plan. Results keep coming, and visible results are rocket fuel for consistency. 3. It protects you from overuse injuries Repeating the same movement pattern loads the same joints and tissues over and over, which is how overuse injuries start. Cross-training spreads the load across different muscle groups and planes of motion. Fewer tweaks and flare-ups means fewer forced breaks, and nothing wrecks a streak like being sidelined. For more ideas, see our guide to the best low-impact exercises to add to your routine . 4. It turns exercise into something you actually enjoy Enjoyment is not fluff. It is the single best predictor of whether you will still be training months from now. Varied routines score higher on enjoyment, autonomy, and self-efficacy, the belief that you can actually do this. When a workout feels like a choice instead of a chore, you stop needing to hunt for motivation every single day. 5. It flexes to real life Some days you have 40 minutes and energy to burn. Some days you have 12 minutes and a toddler. Variety lets you match the workout to the day: a hard interval session when you are fired up, an easy scenic row or walk when you are wiped. A routine that bends to your life is a routine you keep, and this is exactly why so many people ask how to make workouts less boring in the first place. What to vary What it changes Easy example The machine Which muscles and joints do the work Row Monday, ride Wednesday, walk Friday The format Mental engagement and pacing Game one day, coached class the next, scenic route after that The intensity The training stimulus and recovery Hard intervals, then an easy steady session The duration How the workout fits your day 12 minutes when busy, 40 when you are not Same treadmill, dozens of formats: a coached class today, a game tomorrow, a scenic walk the day after. Walk, run, or race a game Aviron Victory Treadmill Incline walks, interval runs, coached classes, and games on one screen, so cardio never turns into a chore. Free 30-day home trial · Financing available Shop the Treadmill → But isn't consistency more important than variety? This is the right question, and the answer is that they are not rivals. Consistency is the goal. Variety is one of the best tools for reaching it. The mistake is thinking you must choose. You do not. It is also worth busting a myth here. "Muscle confusion," the idea that constantly shuffling exercises keeps your muscles guessing, is mostly marketing. Muscles do not get confused. Structured progression and steady practice are the real drivers of results. Randomly changing everything every single day can actually slow you down, because your body never gets to adapt to anything. The sweet spot is a stable framework with planned variety inside it. As a rough guide: Experience level Change the core plan every... But add small variety... Beginner 6 to 12 weeks Session to session (format, game, route) Intermediate 4 to 6 weeks Weekly (intensity and duration) Advanced 3 to 4 weeks Within each session (intervals, targets) In other words, keep the skeleton steady and let the day-to-day workouts stay fresh. That is variety in service of consistency, not against it. How to get variety without buying five machines Here is the practical problem: real variety usually means a gym full of equipment or a closet full of gadgets you will not use. That is expensive, and it reintroduces the friction that made you quit last time. The fix is to put the variety inside the machine instead of across a room full of them. That is the entire idea behind Aviron. Every machine runs the same Engagement Engine: 1,000+ workouts spanning science-backed games, coached classes, streaming, scenic virtual routes, and multiplayer competition, plus 300+ Les Mills workouts. One rower can be a boat race on Monday, a HIIT class on Wednesday, and a calm scenic paddle on Sunday. That is more genuine variety than most people ever get from a gym, without leaving your living room. It is also why fitness entertainment actually works where willpower alone does not. Then there is variety across the whole lineup. Rowing, cycling, and running each bring a different stimulus, so choosing your modality by the day is variety at the highest level. Add the Abs Hero for core-focused sessions and you can cover cardio, strength, and recovery from home. Ride a race, a class, or a route Aviron Fit Bike S Game-powered cycling with classes, scenic rides, and leaderboards to keep every session different. Free 30-day home trial · Financing available Shop the Fit Bike S → The proof it works: 50,000+ members, 4,000,000+ workouts completed, an average rating of 4.8 to 4.9 stars, and 92% of members still training a year later. That is what happens when variety is built in, not bolted on. Frequently asked questions How often should I change my workout routine? Change the core structure of your plan every 4 to 6 weeks for most people. Beginners can wait 6 to 12 weeks to build a foundation, and advanced exercisers may switch every 3 to 4 weeks. Keep smaller variety (formats, games, intensity) going in every session so it never gets stale. Is workout variety the same as muscle confusion? No. "Muscle confusion" is a marketing term, and muscles do not actually get confused. Real workout variety is about training different muscles and movement patterns, staying mentally engaged, and applying progressive overload. The benefits are real; the "confusion" branding is not. Can too much variety hurt your progress? Yes. If you change everything every day, your body never adapts to anything, and progress stalls. The sweet spot is a stable plan with planned variety inside it: same weekly framework, different workouts within it. Does workout variety help beginners or only advanced exercisers? It helps beginners most of all, because beginners are the ones most likely to quit. For a new exerciser, keeping the routine enjoyable and engaging matters more than optimizing every set. Variety is what gets you to the consistency where results are built. What is the easiest way to add variety at home? Change one variable at a time: the format, the intensity, or the length. A machine with built-in games, classes, and scenic routes does this for you automatically, which is the whole point of Aviron's game-powered workouts . If you want a deeper fix for boredom, see how to prevent workout boredom . Make boredom impossible Try any Aviron machine at home. If the variety does not keep you coming back, send it back. title: What is an interview rubric? Build and use guide
summary: Build an interview rubric that panels adopt: define competencies, set calibrated scales and weights, and score candidates on evidence rather than instinct.
body_text: Most interviewers can intuitively grasp the purpose of an interview rubric. The problem is building one your interview panels want to use. To encourage adoption, you need a resource that’s easy for interviewers to implement and makes their jobs easier. In this guide, we’ll walk you through how to build functional interview rubrics that help hiring managers evaluate candidates objectively. Along the way, we’ll define how these rubrics work and what to include to keep scoring consistent. What is an interview rubric? Interview rubrics are structured guides used by interviewers to evaluate different candidates for a role against the same set of job-relevant criteria. A complete rubric has three parts: Competencies: Rubrics detail the skills and ideal behaviors a role requires. They should also provide short definitions for each competency to leave no room for ambiguity. Rating scale: Rubrics include a fixed scale, such as 1–4 or 1–5, where each number on the scale represents a pre-defined meaning. Example benchmarks: Rubrics also include behavioral indicators, short descriptors of what a 2, for example, sounds like when compared to other numbers on the scale. This makes it easier for interviewers to tie what candidates say or demonstrate to a specific score, instead of going off of gut feeling. Interview rubrics vs interview scorecards: What is the difference? While the two terms are often used interchangeably, interview rubrics and scorecards refer to different artifacts in practice. Rubrics are the standard-bearing frameworks for a role. Your team builds them once per role to define competencies, the ratings scale, and example benchmarks. Interview scorecards, on the other hand, are the live documents filled out during the interview to record candidate answers and provide a score. Take the example of an open role with a four-person hiring panel interviewing six candidates. The hiring team creates the rubric first, one time. Then the individual interviewers use the rubric to create 24 different interview scorecards, one for each interview. Why interview rubrics improve hiring Rubrics ensure that candidate-specific evidence is used to drive interviewer recommendations and that the defined job criteria are applied consistently. Some tangible ways rubrics improve hiring include: Quality of hire: Scoring based on pre-defined competencies helps ensure candidates are advanced based on the demonstrative behaviors that predict success in a role, rather than factors like general likeability, pedigree, or a vague sense of cultural fit. Speed and alignment: When panels assess candidates on the same scale, disagreements that arise in the debrief are easier to reconcile, allowing teams to forge alignment and move forward faster. Fairness and compliance: Hiring decisions can be challenged in the future. But using a rubric with defined competencies and scales creates a paper trail that helps panels defend decisions if needed. Candidate experience: Every candidate gets asked the same questions and is held to the same standard, making it easier for interviewers to provide concrete feedback when asked. Common reasons rubrics fail Rubrics don’t usually fail because of some inherent flaw in the competencies selected by hiring panels or the framework they use to score candidates. They fail because rubrics fossilize into untouched documents that never make it into the interview or influence proceedings. Some other common failure points: Vague scales: A scale labeled 1–5 without concrete definitions and examples of behavior or competencies at each step sets up your interviewers to rely on instinct instead of evidence. And relying on instinct can lead to unconscious biases that unfairly skew the hiring process. Misweighted priorities: If the nice-to-have skills carry the same weight as core job requirements, the rubric doesn’t accurately reflect the bar for candidates to clear. Delayed scoring: When interviewers wait until too long after the interview to record scores, solid evidence tends to be replaced by vague impressions. Opinion-based notes: Comments with no evidence behind them ("strong communicator") leave nothing to compare against, so the bar shifts from candidate to candidate depending on who's assessing. What to include in a rubric Rubrics get adopted when they’re specific to roles and encourage interviewers to rely on evidence. Two core sets of elements come together to make that happen. Competencies and question alignment Start by defining core competencies drawn from the job’s requirements, not a template. Finding the right balance is key; include too few competencies, and interviewers will feel it’s missing important context. Too many, and you risk interviewers glossing over them. Each competency should include a short definition and be mapped to specific questions (and vice versa). Build competencies without questions, and you risk interviewers inventing their own inconsistent questions. Build questions without attached competencies, and interviewers end up with potentially helpful information, but no way to map it to the core job requirements in the hiring process. Scoring and evidence fields On the scoring side, rubrics should include the following: Calibrated rating scales: Where each point maps to a written definition. Behavioral indicators: Each point in a score should describe what an answer at that level conveys. Weights: Core competencies that drive success in the role should be properly weighted. Comment fields: For interviewers to easily and consistently record their remarks in one place. Overall scoring ranges: Tie these to a decision, so scores map cleanly to “advance,” “hold,” or “reject” recommendations. How to build and use interview rubrics Building and using your interview rubric is a continuous workflow that extends from role calibration all the way to post-interview review. Here’s how to run it. Build the rubric around competencies and questions Hold a calibration conversation with the hiring manager before you put the first candidate interview on your calendar. Then, ask what success looks like for this new hire in their first six months on the job. That answer informs the core competencies you’ll be hiring for. From there: Define role-specific competencies: In one sentence, if possible, in terms everyone on the interview panel understands. Define score meanings: Articulate what makes a 2 a 2 and a 4 a 4, then fill in the rest of the steps between them on the ratings scale. Assign weights: Work backward from the most essential competencies, making sure core skills and behaviors are highlighted. Write standardized questions: Ensure these are tied to job outcomes, with examples of follow-up prompts in case interviewers need to drill down for evidence. Add a notes field: These should live under each competency and be required for each interviewer to fill out. Use the rubric during and after interviews During the interview, lean on the assessment questions defined in the rubric and use the notes field to actively jot down evidence. Try to capture what candidates say, including verbatim quotes where possible. Then, review the evidence to score the candidate for each competency as soon as the interview ends. The longer you wait to finish scoring, the fuzzier your memory gets, so it’s best to finalize ratings as soon as possible. The evidence that matters most varies depending on the type of role you’re hiring. In an SDR interview, for example, it’s not enough to hear that the candidate is resilient; try to get them to explain in detail how they handle rejection and what they’ve changed specifically in the past when working through a rough sales stretch. For software engineer interviews, on the other hand, you want to understand how candidates approach technical problems—e.g., whether they can articulate any trade-offs between different approaches—not just hear an answer devoid of context. These sorts of deep candidate insights are exactly what rubrics are for and where they prove their value in the evaluation process. Next steps for consistent scoring Teams unlock consistent scoring when they use rubrics to recalibrate their hiring, not just evaluate candidates. The scores a panel produces—and how effectively they achieve alignment—are themselves records of how well a particular rubric performs. As roles, candidate expectations, and markets evolve, reviewing rubrics becomes necessary to ensure they don’t drift from their intended purpose. Calibration and drift review Teams should aim to review rubric data on a quarterly basis, or after a set number of interviews (10–15) for high-volume roles. Three patterns worth keeping an eye out for: Consistently low-scoring competencies: If most or all candidates are routinely earning low marks on a specific competency, odds are good that something is misaligned. Questions might be framed incorrectly, or the bar might be set too high for the role's expected seniority level. Interviewer leniency: If one interviewer on the panel’s candidates are averaging a full point higher than the others’ for their assigned competency, they might be waving candidates along without the proper scrutiny. Score drift across panels: On some panels, scores tend to drift upwards over time when interviewers start comparing candidates against each other, and not the rubric itself. In any of the above scenarios, taking the time to recalibrate with the panel members or retool problem areas in the rubric itself is a valuable intervention that drives improved consistency over time. Operationalizing the rubric Remember: Rubrics earn staying power when they live in the systems your team already uses. Get a few key elements right, and adopting the rubric becomes the path of least resistance. One of these is using embedded score capture in the tools your team already has open. This ensures scorecards get filled out inside the interview window, and not hours (or days) later once recall has already been significantly degraded. Keep one standard-bearing rubric per role. Copying the rubric into a new document for each search allows small tweaks to accumulate over time; eventually, your interviewers are unwittingly working with completely different documents. Filtering reports by competency and user makes those changes visible. Finally, connecting the entire workflow to your ATS keeps scoring history attached to the role, and not stowed away in various team members’ folders. Start with a stronger candidate pool A scoring framework makes your evaluations consistent, but it can only sort the candidates who reach the interview. If the shortlist is thin, better scoring just gives you a clearer view of the same limited options. Let Juicebox handle the sourcing. Describe the role in plain language and Juicebox searches across a large candidate pool to surface best-fit candidates, including the people who aren't applying, so your rubric has stronger candidates to work with. Frequently asked questions What are interview rubrics? Interview rubrics are structured scoring guides used to evaluate candidates against the same set of job-relevant criteria. Rubrics define competencies, assign a rating scale and weights, and provide behavioral indicators describing the type of evidence from candidates that justify a given score. What is a rubric for interviews? A rubric for interviews is the framework a hiring team uses to score candidates. It’s built once per role and used for every candidate in that search. What is an example of an interview rubric? An example rubric for an SDR might measure four competencies: e.g., prospecting approach, objection handling, resilience, and coachability. Each competency will carry a percentage weight that aligns with its importance relative to the others; prospecting might account for 30% of the total, while a lesser factor like coachability would count for 20%. Each competency is anchored by behavioral indicators that help interviewers discern a candidate's score on a set scale, such as 1–4. Lower scores might indicate the candidate answers the question without providing specifics, while higher scores involve a thorough description of the candidate’s experience and aptitude with concrete examples.

title: Innovation at AES

body_text: Innovation at AES AES Next AES Next builds and invests in a portfolio of high-growth businesses and strategic partnerships that drive the global energy transition. By identifying key challenges and opportunities in the energy sector, we apply deep industry expertise to develop and scale breakthrough solutions—from pioneering energy storage to revolutionizing solar deployment—creating tangible value for our company, partners, and communities. AES Next Portfolio AES Next follows a proven approach to identity, select, develop and scale strategic business opportunities to create long-term value for our business, our partners and the industry. Maximo: revolutionizing solar installation through robotics To keep up with increased energy demand, AES developed Maximo, the first AI-enabled solar robot for the end-to-end installation of solar modules. Skilled construction crews rely on Maximo to improve speed and safety by automating the strenuous heavy lifting of solar panels to accelerate solar installation. title: Form with conditionals vs. multiple forms in the same card: which organization should you choose?
summary: See when to use a form with conditionals and when to use multiple forms in the same open card in Jestor.
body_text: In Jestor , an open card can either have a single form with conditional fields that appear or disappear based on set rules, or several independent forms in different side panels, each with its own purpose. When an overly long form gets in the way More complex processes — like multi-step approvals or record-heavy intake forms — suffer when everything sits in a single long form, even if it's well organized with conditionals. That forces the user to scroll through the entire screen to find the right section, even when most of that information isn't relevant at the moment they're working on the record. How to decide which organization to use Use conditionals in a single form when there are just a few, related sections. Use multiple forms when the card brings together very different audiences or stages. Split into separate forms information that only makes sense for distinct roles, like requester and approver. Customize color and style for each separate form, for visual identification. Set one of the forms as read-only, if that fits the process. Organization Structure Best for Single form with conditionals One form, fields appear/disappear based on rules A few, related sections Multiple forms on the card Independent side panels, each with its own purpose Very different audiences or stages on the same card Why choose Jestor? Jestor applies the same conditional, permission, and capability rules already used in superforms to multiple forms on a card, so splitting the card into parts doesn't mean losing any customization already available on the platform. Frequently Asked Questions Can each separate form have a different color for visual identification? Yes, you can customize the color and style of each form separately within the same card. Do conditionals work the same way in separate forms as in a single form? Yes, the same conditional rules apply, whether they're in a single form or split across several. Can I set one of the forms as read-only? Yes, you can configure each separate form as editable or read-only.
